They flee from me, that sometime did me seek With naked foot, stalking in my chamber. I have seen them gentle, tame, and meek, That now are wild, and do not remember That sometime they put themselves in danger To take bread at my hand; and now they range Busily seeking with a continual change. Thanked be fortune it hath been otherwise Twenty times better; but once, in special, In thin array, after a pleasant guise, When her loose gown from her shoulders did fall, And she me caught in her arms long and small; Therewith all sweetly did me kiss, And softly said, ‘Dear heart, how like you this?’ It was no dream: I lay broad waking: But all is turned, thorough my gentleness, Into a strange fashion of forsaking; And I have leave to go of her goodness, And she also to use newfangleness. But since that I so kindly am served, I would fain know what she hath deserved.

Those who once pursued me now run away, once creeping barefoot right into my bedroom. I remember when they were kind, calm, and obedient, but now they've grown untamed and have forgotten how they once took the risk of coming close to eat bread from my hand. These days they wander off, endlessly busy and constantly shifting.

I'm grateful to fortune that things weren't always this way—there were times far better, twenty times over. One occasion stands out especially: she came dressed lightly, in a charming manner, and her loose gown slipped from her shoulders. She wrapped me in her slender, encircling arms, kissed me tenderly, and whispered gently, "My darling, how do you enjoy this?"

None of this was a dream—I was fully awake as I lay there. Yet everything has changed. Because of my own kindness, I've been abandoned in a peculiar way. Thanks to her so-called generosity, I'm now free to leave, and she's equally free to chase after new attractions. But since I've been treated in such a manner, I'd genuinely like to know what fate she truly deserves.

# They Who Once Sought Me

There was a time when those who now avoid me would seek me out with eagerness and desire. The speaker looks back on that vanished season with sorrow, mourning how the very people who once pursued him have fled from his presence and left him entirely alone. Where he was once surrounded by attention and affection, he now finds only absence and neglect.

He remembers his former lovers as gentle and tame creatures, willing to draw near despite the dangers such closeness might bring. They took risks to be with him, stepping softly toward him with meekness and trust. Yet that tenderness has not lasted. Those same lovers have since grown wild and unpredictable, ranging far from him and forgetting the intimacy they once shared. What was once close and familiar has become distant and strange.

Among these memories, one encounter stands out with particular vividness. He recalls a woman who came to him and embraced him warmly, her clothing loosening as she leaned close. She kissed him tenderly and, with a sweet and gentle voice, asked him how he liked her affection. The moment was one of unexpected softness and intimacy, an experience so striking that it has remained with him ever since.

The speaker is careful to insist that this memory was no fantasy or illusion. It was real, waking experience, not a dream conjured by longing. And yet, for all its truth, everything has since transformed. The warmth of that encounter has given way to a strange and bewildering kind of abandonment, leaving him to wonder how something so genuine could dissolve so completely.

In the end, he reflects with bitterness on his situation. Despite his own gentleness and kindness, he has been cast aside and forgotten. His former lover, so quick to change and so free in her affections, has moved on without him. He is left to consider what such fickleness truly deserves, questioning whether her inconstancy should meet with reward or with the same neglect she has shown to him.

# They Flee From Me

The poem opens with a wistful meditation on absence. The speaker recalls a time when others sought him out willingly, coming to him with a kind of trembling eagerness. He compares these former lovers to wild creatures—gentle, tame, and unafraid—who once approached his chamber, took bread from his hand, and risked exposure to be near him. Now, however, these same figures flee, wandering elsewhere and forgetting the intimacy they once so freely offered. The imagery of once-tame animals now returned to their wildness underscores the transformation from devotion to indifference, and the speaker registers this change with a mixture of nostalgia and sorrow.

As the poem turns inward, the speaker acknowledges that better fortune once smiled upon him. There was a season when he was favored, when love and circumstance both seemed to reward him. But those days have passed, and the memory of abundance only sharpens the ache of present neglect. The tone shifts from general reflection to a single, vivid recollection—one particular encounter that lingers in the speaker's mind with startling clarity.

He remembers a moment of unexpected boldness, when his lover came to him in loose and inviting attire, embracing him and drawing him close. In a soft voice she asked how he liked this display of tenderness. The memory is rendered with sensual immediacy, and for a brief moment the poem recovers the warmth and passion of that intimate exchange. The recollection is not a dream, the speaker insists—it truly happened, and its reality makes the subsequent loss all the more painful.

Yet the sweetness of memory quickly curdles into bitterness. The speaker reflects on how thoroughly the intimacy has been abandoned, how his lover's gentleness has given way to a strange and studied distance. He notes, with wounded irony, that she has taken advantage of his own good nature—his willingness to let her come and go freely—and repaid his openness with faithlessness. The freedom he granted has become the very means of his betrayal.

The poem closes on a note of bitter interrogation. Having been forsaken, the speaker turns the situation over in his mind and poses a pointed final question: since his lover has treated him so unkindly and proven so inconstant, what does she deserve in return? The question hangs unanswered, its bitterness left to resonate. In these closing lines, the poem captures not only the specific pain of one betrayal but a broader disillusionment—an awareness of how easily affection fades, how fickle both love and fortune can prove, and how those who once pursued us most ardently may become the ones who wound us most deeply.
